title: Roads, Trails, and Rails West

sheetTitle.es: Caminos, senderos y ferrocarriles hacia el Oeste

summary: Follow the trails settlers took west in the 1800s, see whose lands they crossed, and find out how railroads replaced the wagon trails.
subject: History
alsoFits: Sectional economies: industry, cities and immigration
studentLogin: Not needed to explore the map

image.alt: Preview of the Roads, Trails, and Rails West map

layers.name: Trails West
layers.shows: Seven trails west: Oregon, California, Mormon Pioneer, Old Spanish, Santa Fe, Butterfield Overland and Pony Express, each a dotted line in its own color in the legend. Each pop-up is titled with the trail's name and gives a short history with places, dates and distances.
layers.source: National Geographic Education, from National Park Service trail information

layers.name: Transcontinental Railroads completed by 1911
layers.shows: Five transcontinental lines as thick colored lines named in the legend: Great Northern, Northern Pacific, Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific), Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific) and Southern Pacific. No pop-up. In the Railroads group.
layers.source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team

layers.name: Railroads 1826 to 1911
layers.shows: All railroad lines built from 1826 to 1911, as thin gray lines. Each pop-up gives the railroad's name (where recorded) and the year it was in operation by. In the Railroads group.
layers.source: Jeremy Atack, historical railroad data (ICPSR 36353), prepared by the MapMaker team

layers.name: Indigenous Territories
layers.shows: Approximate territories of Indigenous nations, from a community-made map, each shaded in its own color with the nation's name appearing when zoomed in. Not listed in the legend. No pop-up.

knownIssues.note: Gives the years 1840 to 1860, then says many travelers were "fleeing the American Civil War (1861-1865)", which began after that period.

compellingQuestion.en: How did trails and then railroads change the American West, and for whom?
compellingQuestion.es: ¿Cómo cambiaron los senderos, y después los ferrocarriles, el Oeste de Estados Unidos, y para quién?

questions.task: Click three trails (use the legend to tell them apart) and note from each pop-up where the trail started and ended. Most began in Missouri: why there?
frontOfClass: Open the legend and show the seven trail colours.
Click the dotted Oregon trail line and read where it started and ended.
Click the Santa Fe trail and read where it started.
Click the Pony Express trail and read where it started.
Ask: in which state do most of the trails start?
Ask: looking at the map, why there?

steps.en: Open the legend to see which color is which trail.
steps.es: Abre la leyenda para ver qué color corresponde a cada sendero.

steps.en: Click three of the dotted trail lines.
steps.es: Haz clic en tres de las líneas punteadas de los senderos.

steps.en: Read in each pop-up where the trail started and ended.
steps.es: Lee en cada ventana emergente dónde empezaba y terminaba el sendero.

ask.en: Where did each trail start and end? In which state do most of the trails start?
ask.es: ¿Dónde empezaba y terminaba cada sendero? ¿En qué estado empiezan la mayoría de los senderos?

answer.where: Trails West pop-ups (title is the trail name, the text gives the places). Most trails start in Missouri: Independence (Oregon, California), St. Joseph (Pony Express), St. Louis (Butterfield Overland) or Missouri in general (Santa Fe). On the map, the Mormon Pioneer trail's eastern end is at Nauvoo, Illinois, on the Mississippi, and its pop-up mentions Nauvoo and Omaha.

table.caption: Where the trails started and ended, from their pop-ups and the map
rows: Willamette River valley, near Portland, Oregon
Nauvoo, Illinois (the line's eastern end on the map), then past Omaha, Nebraska
St. Louis, Missouri, and Memphis, Tennessee, via Fort Smith, Arkansas

answer.accept: Missouri. For why, a good answer uses the map: Missouri was at the western edge of the settled states and on the Missouri River, so it was the last place to buy supplies and the river was the way in.

questions.task: Open the Oregon Trail pop-up for its length and how many people used it. Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri (on the basemap, just east of Kansas City), to Portland, Oregon, and compare it with the trail's length.
frontOfClass: Click the Oregon trail line and read its length and how many people used it.
Zoom in on Kansas City and find Independence, Missouri, on the basemap.
Use Measure in miles from Independence to Portland, Oregon.
Ask: how much longer is the trail than the straight line?
Trace the dotted Oregon line from Independence to Portland with the pointer.
Ask: why is the trail so much longer than a straight line?

steps.en: Find the Oregon Trail's color in the legend.
steps.es: Busca el color del sendero de Oregón en la leyenda.

steps.en: Click the Oregon Trail and read its length and how many people traveled it.
steps.es: Haz clic en el sendero de Oregón y lee su longitud y cuántas personas lo recorrieron.

steps.en: Find Independence, Missouri, on the basemap, next to Kansas City.
steps.es: Busca Independence, Misuri, en el mapa base, junto a Kansas City.

steps.en: Use Measure for a straight line from Independence to Portland, Oregon.
steps.es: Usa la herramienta de medir (Measure) para trazar una línea recta de Independence a Portland, Oregón.

ask.en: How long was the Oregon Trail, and how many people traveled it? Why is the trail longer than a straight line?
ask.es: ¿Qué longitud tenía el sendero de Oregón y cuántas personas lo recorrieron? ¿Por qué el sendero es más largo que una línea recta?

fill.en: Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon: ________ miles
fill.es: Mide la distancia en línea recta de Independence (Misuri) a Portland (Oregón): ________ millas

answer.where: Oregon Trail pop-up: about 2,000 miles (3,219 km); 300,000 to 400,000 people between 1840 and 1860. Measure tool, Independence to Portland: about 1,500 miles (accept 1,450 to 1,550).
answer.accept: The trail is about 500 miles longer than the straight line. A good answer says the dotted line bends to follow rivers (the pop-up names the Platte, North Platte, Snake and Columbia) for water and grass, and crosses the mountains through passes rather than straight over them.

questions.task: Turn on Indigenous Territories in Map layers and zoom in until the nations' names appear, then follow one trail from end to end. Was the West empty land when the trails were built? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn on Indigenous Territories.
Zoom in until the nations' names appear along the Oregon trail.
Trace the Oregon trail from Independence to Portland, reading out the names it crosses.
Ask: was the land the trail crossed empty?
Ask: what might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn on Indigenous Territories.
steps.es: En las capas del mapa (Map layers), activa Indigenous Territories (territorios indígenas).

steps.en: Zoom in until the nations' names appear.
steps.es: Acércate hasta que aparezcan los nombres de las naciones.

steps.en: Follow one trail from one end to the other.
steps.es: Sigue un sendero de un extremo al otro.

steps.en: Find two nations whose land it crossed.
steps.es: Busca dos naciones cuyas tierras cruzaba.

ask.en: Which two nations' land did the trail cross? Was the land the trail crossed empty? What might the trail have meant for the people who lived there?
ask.es: ¿Las tierras de qué dos naciones cruzaba el sendero? ¿Estaba vacía la tierra que cruzaba el sendero? ¿Qué pudo significar el sendero para las personas que vivían allí?

answer.where: Indigenous Territories layer (off at start; names draw when zoomed in). Any trail runs through a continuous patchwork of shaded territories from Missouri to the coast; for example the Oregon Trail crosses lands labeled for the Kaw, Pawnee, Lakota, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Shoshone, Nez Perce and others. Accept any two names read from the map.
answer.accept: No, the land was not empty: the layer shows nations' territories along the whole trail. For the second part, a good answer reasons from the map that hundreds of thousands of travelers, their wagons and animals crossed these lands, so it could mean lost hunting grounds and grass, disease, pressure on water, forts and settlements along the route, and later loss of the land itself; any reasoned effect, positive or negative, that connects the trail to the people living there is acceptable.

title.es: De los senderos a los rieles

questions.task: Turn on the Railroads group in Map layers. Using the legend, which trails does the Union Pacific and Central Pacific line follow most closely? Click a thin gray railroad line to see when it was in operation (the thick transcontinental lines have no pop-up).
frontOfClass: In Map layers, turn on Railroads.
Open the legend and find Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific).
Trace the two thick lines from Omaha to Sacramento.
Ask: which dotted trails do they follow most closely?
Click a thin gray railroad line and read the year it was in operation by.
Ask: what happened to the wagon trails once the railroad opened?

steps.en: In Map layers, turn on Railroads.
steps.es: En las capas del mapa (Map layers), activa Railroads (ferrocarriles).

steps.en: Use the legend to find the Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and (Central Pacific) lines.
steps.es: Usa la leyenda para encontrar las líneas Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) y (Central Pacific).

steps.en: Click a thin gray railroad line and read when it was in operation by.
steps.es: Haz clic en una línea gris fina de ferrocarril y lee desde cuándo funcionaba.

ask.en: Which trails do the Transcontinental Railroad lines follow most closely? By when was the gray railroad line in operation?
ask.es: ¿Qué senderos siguen más de cerca las líneas del Transcontinental Railroad? ¿Desde cuándo funcionaba la línea gris de ferrocarril?

answer.where: Legend: Transcontinental Railroad (Union Pacific) and Transcontinental Railroad (Central Pacific) are thick colored lines running from Omaha across Nebraska, Wyoming, Utah and Nevada to Sacramento. Compare with the dotted California and Mormon Pioneer trails (and the Pony Express across Nevada). Railroads 1826 to 1911 pop-up: "Railroad in operation by:" followed by a year; any year the student reads is fine. The California Trail pop-up says the trail was used until 1869, when the transcontinental railroad was completed.
answer.accept: The California and Mormon Pioneer trails (also the Pony Express across Nevada). A good answer notes the railroad runs along the same river valleys and passes the wagon trails used, and gives a year read from a gray line's pop-up.

final.teacher: Students answer with evidence from at least two layers. Some ways to do it: a paragraph, one journey sketched on the map with notes (sketches are not saved, so students should screenshot or describe them), or a short talk using the map.

student.en: Answer the big question using evidence from at least two layers on the map. You can write a paragraph, sketch on the map, or both.
student.es: Responde la pregunta central con evidencia de al menos dos capas del mapa. Puedes escribir un párrafo, dibujar en el mapa o hacer ambas cosas.

objectives: Identify where three of the seven trails started and ended from their pop-ups, and explain from the map why most began in Missouri.
Measure the straight-line distance from Independence, Missouri, to Portland, Oregon, and compare it with the Oregon Trail's length in its pop-up.
Name Indigenous nations whose lands a trail crossed, using the Indigenous Territories layer.
Compare the transcontinental railroad lines in the legend with the dotted trails to see which routes the railroads followed.
Use evidence from at least two layers to explain how trails and then railroads changed the West, and for whom.
discussion: The Oregon Trail is about 500 miles longer than the straight line you measured. What did the dotted line follow instead, and what does that say about what a wagon party needed most?
With Indigenous Territories turned on, how did the map change for you? What might a trail have meant for the people whose lands it crossed, and whose story does the Trails West layer leave out?

The Union Pacific and Central Pacific lines run close to the California and Mormon Pioneer trails. Why might the railroad builders have chosen the same route, and what happened to the trails once the railroad opened?

differentiation.support: Do question 1 together from the front, and write the seven trail names with their legend colours on the board so students can find each line.
differentiation.stretch: With Indigenous Territories and Railroads both on, ask whether the Union Pacific and Central Pacific line crosses the same nations' lands as the trails, and what that meant for those nations.

resources.title: History & Culture, Oregon National Historic Trail
Primary Source Set: Westward Expansion: Encounters at a Cultural Crossroads

beforeYouStart.en: In the 1800s, hundreds of thousands of people from the eastern United States went west in wagons, looking for farmland, gold or a place to practice their religion freely. A journey along one of the trails could take months. Later in the century, railroads were built across the West.
beforeYouStart.es: En el siglo XIX, cientos de miles de personas del este de Estados Unidos viajaron al Oeste en carretas, en busca de tierras de cultivo, oro o un lugar donde practicar su religión libremente. Un viaje por uno de los senderos podía durar meses. Más adelante en ese siglo, se construyeron ferrocarriles a través del Oeste.

readingTheMap.en: Each trail is a dotted line in its own color; the legend names them, and clicking a trail opens its pop-up. City and state names are part of the basemap. Railroads and Indigenous Territories are off when the map opens: turn them on in Map layers. Thick colored lines are the transcontinental railroads, named in the legend, and thin gray lines are other railroads; only the thin gray lines have pop-ups. Each Indigenous nation's territory is shaded in its own color, and its name appears when you zoom in. The territories are approximate and aren't listed in the legend.
readingTheMap.es: Cada sendero es una línea punteada de un color distinto; la leyenda indica sus nombres, y al hacer clic en un sendero se abre su ventana emergente. Los nombres de ciudades y estados forman parte del mapa base. Las capas Railroads e Indigenous Territories están desactivadas al abrir el mapa: actívalas en las capas del mapa (Map layers). Las líneas gruesas de colores son los ferrocarriles transcontinentales, con sus nombres en la leyenda, y las líneas grises finas son otros ferrocarriles; solo las líneas grises finas tienen ventana emergente. El territorio de cada nación indígena tiene su propio color, y su nombre aparece al acercarte. Los territorios son aproximados y no aparecen en la leyenda.

reflection.en: What did the map show you about the journey west that you might not have noticed from reading alone?
reflection.es: ¿Qué te mostró el mapa sobre el viaje al Oeste que quizá no habrías notado solo con la lectura?

teacherNotes.beforeClass: The Railroads group and Indigenous Territories are off when the map opens; students turn them on in Map layers for questions 3 and 4. There are no bookmarks, so students zoom and pan to the trails themselves.

misconceptions.claim: The West was empty before settlers arrived.
misconceptions.response: The Indigenous Territories layer shows nations' lands across the whole region the trails crossed.

misconceptions.claim: Everyone went west on the Oregon Trail.
misconceptions.response: The map shows seven trails, to Oregon, California, Utah, New Mexico and Southern California.

misconceptions.claim: The Pony Express lasted for decades.
misconceptions.response: Its pop-up says it ran for 18 months, from April 1860 to October 1861.

standards.text: Explain the political, economic, and social roots of Manifest Destiny
Analyze the relationship between the concept of Manifest Destiny and the westward growth of the nation
Analyze how physical characteristics of the environment influenced population distribution, settlement patterns, and economic activities in the United States during the 17th, 18th, and 19th centuries
Examine the causes, course, and consequences of United States westward expansion and its growing diplomatic assertiveness
Explain how changes in transportation and communication technology influence the spatial connections among human settlements and affect the diffusion of ideas and cultural practices
Explain multiple causes and effects of events and developments in the past
